procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated January 23, 1968 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Revision No. 91 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant's revision petition before the High Court was summarily rejected.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave granted by the Court.

directions: The order of forfeiture of foodgrains is also set aside.
If any money has been recovered by sale of the foodgrains, it shall be handed over to the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether unregistered lease deeds, inadmissible under the Registration Act for certain purposes, can be considered in a criminal prosecution for the collateral purpose of showing that the accused held land for cultivation.

facts: The appellant was prosecuted under the Essential Commodities Act for storing foodgrains in quantities larger than permitted without a license.
The appellant's defense was that he was an agriculturist and had grown the foodgrains himself on leased land.
To support his defense, he produced oral testimony and several unregistered lease deeds.
The trial court rejected the deeds, ruling they were inadmissible as evidence under s. 49 of the Registration Act because they were not registered.
law: The Supreme Court distinguished the standard of evidence required in a criminal prosecution from that in a civil case concerning property rights.
It held that in a criminal case, the primary question regarding evidence is whether it is genuine and whether an inference of innocence can be based upon it.
The Court established that documents that are inadmissible for their primary purpose due to lack of registration can still be used for a "collateral purpose."
application: The Court reasoned that the unregistered lease deeds, while not admissible to prove the legal validity of the leases themselves, could serve the collateral purpose of corroborating the oral evidence.
Specifically, the deeds showed that the lands the witnesses testified about were the same lands the appellant claimed to hold for cultivation.
By serving this collateral purpose, the deeds supported the appellant's defense that he was an agriculturist.
If he was an agriculturist, he was exempt from the presumption under the law that the stored grain was for the purpose of sale.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that in a criminal prosecution, the unregistered lease deeds were admissible for the collateral purpose of showing that the accused held land for cultivation, thereby supporting his defense that he was an agriculturist and exempt from the charges.

issue.issue_text: Whether the testimony of witnesses can be rejected solely on the ground that they are neighbours of the accused and thus presumed to be interested parties.

facts: The appellant, accused of illegally storing foodgrains, presented oral evidence from witnesses to prove he was an agriculturist.
The trial magistrate and the Sessions Judge rejected the testimony of these witnesses.
law: The lower courts rejected the testimony on the basis that the witnesses were the appellant's next-door neighbors and, as such, were presumed to be interested parties who would have a "soft corner for him."
application: The Supreme Court found that the lower courts had not provided adequate reasons for rejecting the testimony.
The Court questioned why the evidence of a next-door neighbor should be automatically rejected.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that there is no reason to reject the testimony of a witness solely on the ground that they are a neighbor of the accused. Such evidence can only be rejected if there is something "intrinsically wrong with that evidence" itself.

issue.issue_text: Whether the presumption under Clause 3(2) of the Bihar Foodgrain Dealer's Licensing Order 1966, that storage of foodgrains above a certain quantity is for the purpose of sale, can be drawn against an accused who has successfully proved that he is an agriculturist.

facts: An individual (the appellant) was found storing foodgrains in quantities exceeding the limits permitted by the Bihar Foodgrain Dealer's Licensing Order, 1966.
He was prosecuted under the Essential Commodities Act for violating the Order.
The appellant's defense was that he was an agriculturist and the grains were from his own cultivation on leased lands.
He presented evidence, including unregistered lease deeds and oral testimony from witnesses (his neighbors), to prove he was an agriculturist.
The lower courts rejected this evidence, deeming the deeds inadmissible because they were unregistered and the witnesses unreliable because they were neighbors.
law: Clause 3(2) of the Bihar Foodgrain Dealer's Licensing Order, 1966, establishes a legal presumption.
This presumption states that any person (other than a bona fide consumer or an agriculturist) who stores foodgrains above a certain quantity is presumed to be storing them for the purpose of sale.
Crucially, the clause explicitly excludes agriculturists from this presumption.
application: The Supreme Court re-evaluated the evidence that the lower courts had rejected.

It held that the unregistered lease deeds, while perhaps not admissible to prove property title, were valid for the "collateral purpose" of showing that the appellant held land for cultivation in a criminal proceeding.

The Court also found no valid reason to reject the testimony of the appellant's neighbors simply because of their proximity, stating their evidence should only be rejected if there is something "intrinsically wrong" with it.
Based on the totality of the evidence (lease deeds, receipts, and oral testimony), the Court concluded that the appellant had successfully proven that he was, in fact, an agriculturist.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that because the appellant had successfully proved he was an agriculturist, he fell under the explicit exemption provided in Clause 3(2) of the Order. Consequently, the legal presumption that he was storing the foodgrains for the purpose of sale could not be drawn against him. Without this presumption, the prosecution's case against him was unproven, and his conviction was set aside.

arguments.issue_text: Whether unregistered lease deeds, inadmissible under the Registration Act for certain purposes, can be considered in a criminal prosecution for the collateral purpose of showing that the accused held land for cultivation.
appellant_arguments: The unregistered lease deeds, while perhaps inadmissible for proving the lease itself, should be considered for the collateral purpose of showing that the appellant held land for cultivation.
The deeds, along with oral testimony, support the defense that the appellant is an agriculturist and the foodgrains were his own produce.
respondent_arguments: The lease deeds are inadmissible in evidence under Section 49 of the Registration Act because they are not registered.
The documents are unreliable as they could have been brought into existence at any time to create a false defense.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the testimony of witnesses can be rejected solely on the ground that they are neighbours of the accused and thus presumed to be interested parties.
appellant_arguments: The oral evidence from witnesses who testified that he was an agriculturist cultivating 80-90 bighas of land should be accepted.
There is no valid reason to reject the testimony of witnesses simply because they are neighbors; their evidence should only be rejected if it is intrinsically flawed.
respondent_arguments: The testimony of the witnesses is unreliable because they are the appellant's next-door neighbors and are therefore interested parties with a 'soft corner' for him.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the presumption under Clause 3(2) of the Bihar Foodgrain Dealer's Licensing Order 1966, that storage of foodgrains above a certain quantity is for the purpose of sale, can be drawn against an accused who has successfully proved that he is an agriculturist.
appellant_arguments: The appellant is an agriculturist, and the foodgrains found were grown by him on leased lands.
As an agriculturist, he is expressly excluded from the presumption under Clause 3(2) that the stored grains were for the purpose of sale as a dealer.
respondent_arguments: The case against the appellant is based on the presumption in Clause 3(2) of the Order.
Since the appellant stored foodgrains above the permitted quantities, the presumption that he is a dealer storing them for sale should be applied, leading to his conviction.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In a criminal prosecution, unregistered documents, such as lease-deeds, which may be inadmissible for other purposes under the Registration Act, can be considered for the collateral purpose of supporting a defense and determining if an inference of innocence can be drawn from them.
obiter: Carrying on of business may be found in one instance or more, depending upon the circumstances of the case, as even a single transaction can be demonstrated to be in the course of business.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant successfully proved that he is an agriculturist, and therefore, the presumption under Clause 3(2) of the Bihar Foodgrain Dealer's Licensing Order 1966—that the stored foodgrains were for the purpose of sale as a dealer—could not be drawn against him. The court found that the evidence, including unregistered lease deeds admitted for the collateral purpose of showing he held land for cultivation and oral testimony from witnesses who were improperly discredited merely for being neighbors, established his status as an agriculturist. Since agriculturists are expressly excluded from the presumption and that presumption was the basis of the prosecution, the case against him was unproven and his conviction was improper.
legal_tests_applied: Unregistered documents, while inadmissible for proving the primary transaction (like a lease), can be considered in a criminal prosecution for the collateral purpose of showing that the accused held land for cultivation.

The testimony of a witness cannot be rejected solely on the ground of their relationship to the accused, such as being a neighbor; it can only be rejected if there is something intrinsically wrong with the evidence itself.

A statutory presumption cannot be drawn against an accused who successfully proves they fall into a category expressly excluded by the statute. In this case, once the appellant proved he was an agriculturist, the presumption that he stored grain for sale as a dealer could not be applied.
policy_considerations: The court reinforces the principle of fair evidence evaluation by stating that a witness's testimony, such as that of a neighbor, should not be dismissed based on a presumed bias but must be assessed on its own merits and rejected only if intrinsically flawed.
